opus-5.5.text:
I think those papers are incredibly valuable, and honestly, I'd say they're among the most important contributions in the whole line of work. When you put out a claim like the lottery ticket hypothesis, you're making a bet about how neural networks behave, and the only way we find out whether that bet holds up is if other people go and poke at it, try it in settings I didn't think of, and see where it breaks.

And it did break in places. The original experiments were on fairly small networks, things like MNIST and CIFAR-10, and when people tried to scale it up to bigger networks and harder tasks, the simple version of the procedure, rewinding all the way back to initialization, just didn't work. Some of the papers that pointed this out were pretty pointed about it, and that was completely fair. That pushback is a big part of what led us to the work on rewinding to an early point in training rather than to iteration zero, and to thinking about linear mode connectivity and stability to SGD noise. So the criticism didn't just correct the record; it actually produced a better understanding of what was going on.

I'll be honest that, on a personal level, it's not always fun to read a paper whose purpose is essentially to say "this claim you made doesn't hold up." There's a natural defensive instinct. But I think the right attitude is to treat that as the field working the way it's supposed to. Science isn't about any one person being right; it's about the community converging on what's true. If my work gets refined or even partially overturned, and we end up knowing more than we did before, that's a win.

What I do care about is that the scrutiny is done carefully and in good faith: that people are precise about which claim they're testing, under what conditions, and that they distinguish between "this doesn't happen in this setting" and "this phenomenon doesn't exist." Some of the best critical papers were very careful in exactly that way, and they made the whole area more rigorous. I'd much rather be in a subfield where people take each other's claims seriously enough to try to break them than one where everyone just cites each other and moves on.

r001.rationale: The response values others testing and challenging claims, but does not identify authors’ insufficient efforts to falsify their own results as a weakness.

r002.rationale: It describes scrutiny as part of science and says it can make the area more rigorous, but does not frame this as restoring discipline after wishful thinking shaped research claims.

r003.rationale: It says criticism can refine understanding, but does not explain that insufficiently rigorous work leaves authors vulnerable to years-later public refutation by more careful researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're essential, honestly, and I say that as someone whose work has been on the receiving end of them. When Michael Carbin and I put out the original lottery ticket paper, it was a set of experiments on small networks and a hypothesis. That's all it was. A hypothesis is only useful if people try to break it, and the papers that came after and said "this doesn't hold at scale," or "the mask matters but the initialization doesn't," or "random reinitialization works just as well in these settings" were doing exactly what science is supposed to do.

The Liu et al. "Rethinking the Value of Network Pruning" paper is a good example. They showed that for a lot of structured pruning setups, you could just train the pruned architecture from scratch and match the results. That was uncomfortable to read at first, but it was correct for the regimes they studied, and it pushed us to be much more careful about where the phenomenon actually shows up. It's part of why we ended up doing the rewinding work and the linear mode connectivity work, because we had to answer the question: when does this actually hold, and why? We wouldn't have gotten there without people pushing back.

I'd also say the field has a bit of a problem where a catchy name and a clean story can outrun the evidence. "Lottery ticket" is a very evocative phrase. People started citing it as if it were an established fact about all neural networks, when the original claims were much narrower. So the scrutiny papers serve a second function, which is calibration. They remind everyone, including me, what has actually been shown versus what's been speculated.

The one thing I'd push on is that scrutiny has to be done carefully too. There were a few replication attempts that drew strong conclusions from setups that differed from the original in ways that mattered, and that can muddy things as much as overclaiming does. But on balance, I'd much rather be in a community that over-scrutinizes than one that takes results on faith. If the hypothesis is wrong, I want to know. If it's right in a narrower form than I originally thought, which I think is where we've landed, I want to know that too.

r001.rationale: The candidate says other researchers should try to disprove the hypothesis, but does not identify the lottery ticket authors’ failure to try to falsify their own results as a weakness.

r002.rationale: The candidate says scrutiny helps calibrate claims that outran the evidence, but does not frame this as restoring scientific discipline where wishful thinking shaped the claims.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses later scrutiny and refutation, but does not say insufficiently rigorous research leaves authors exposed to public refutation for years.

astra-6.text:
I think those papers are incredibly valuable. If we make a claim, other people should scrutinize it, try to reproduce it, and figure out where it breaks down. That’s how we learn what’s actually going on. And with lottery tickets, there are a lot of details that matter: what network you’re using, how you train it, what you mean by a ticket. A result that challenges a claim can help us understand its scope much more precisely.

Of course, it can be uncomfortable when it’s your work being challenged. You put a lot of yourself into a paper. But I want to know if something is wrong, or if the story is more complicated than we thought. The goal isn’t to defend the original hypothesis at all costs; it’s to understand neural networks. If somebody gives us a better explanation, that’s progress.

r002.rationale: It describes critical papers as helping clarify claims, but does not connect them to restoring scientific discipline or correcting wishful thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those papers are incredibly valuable. If we put a claim out there, people should scrutinize it, try to reproduce it, and figure out where it breaks down. That’s how we learn what’s actually going on.

With lottery tickets, there are a lot of details that matter: what network you’re using, how you’re training it, what you mean by a winning ticket. A paper that challenges a result can help us understand which of those details are essential and where we’ve stated something too broadly. I might disagree with a particular interpretation, but I want people doing that work. The goal is to understand these networks, and that requires being willing to have our explanations challenged.
